title: RTOS, Interrupts & Concurrency
description: Review of interrupt handling, tasks and scheduling, shared data, timing analysis, and the RTOS configuration.

items.text: Interrupt priorities are assigned deliberately and documented
items.hint: Including which priorities may call RTOS functions (e.g. configMAX_SYSCALL_INTERRUPT_PRIORITY).

items.text: Interrupt handlers are short, and defer work to tasks or the main loop
items.hint: Measure the worst-case ISR time. Long ISRs delay everything below them.

items.text: Interrupts are cleared correctly, with no lost or repeated events
items.hint: Clear before return and allow for the write-buffer delay on Cortex-M parts.

items.text: Critical sections that disable interrupts are short and measured
items.hint: Worst-case interrupt latency is the longest critical section plus the higher-priority ISRs.

items.text: Unused interrupt vectors go to a handler that logs and resets
items.hint: Not an empty infinite loop that looks like a hang.

items.text: Each task's purpose, priority, period, and stack size are listed in one place
items.hint: A table in the architecture doc, kept in sync with the code.

items.text: Worst-case response times meet the timing requirements
items.hint: Measure with a trace tool (e.g. SystemView, Tracealyzer) under full load.

items.text: Blocking calls have timeouts, and the timeout case is handled
items.hint: portMAX_DELAY should be rare and justified.

items.text: CPU load is measured, with margin at peak
items.hint: Idle-task time under the worst realistic load. Keep headroom for future features.

items.text: RTOS configuration options are reviewed (tick rate, assert, stack checking, run-time stats)
items.hint: Turn on configASSERT and stack checking in all builds that are tested.

items.text: The main loop's worst-case cycle time meets every deadline it serves
items.hint: In a superloop, one slow function delays everything. Measure the longest pass.

items.text: Data shared between tasks or with ISRs is protected or provably atomic
items.hint: Mutex, critical section, queue, or a single-writer design. volatile alone doesn't make access atomic.

items.text: Lock ordering is defined, so there are no deadlocks
items.hint: Document the order. Never take a mutex inside an ISR.

items.text: Priority inversion is prevented where a low-priority task holds a shared resource
items.hint: Use mutexes with priority inheritance, not binary semaphores.

items.text: Queue and buffer depths are sized for bursts, and overflow is detected and counted
items.hint: A full queue drops data silently unless the code checks the return value.

items.text: Non-reentrant library calls are not used from several contexts
items.hint: E.g. strtok, some printf implementations, and newlib's malloc without locks.
